intro: Making an appointment, saying where it hurts, describing your symptoms, understanding the doctor’s advice and buying medicine at the pharmacy: these situations need exact words. This lesson gives you the key structures (I’ve got a…, My… hurts, I feel…) and advice with “should” (lesson 56). Of course, it does not replace medical advice.
objectifs: Make an appointment with a doctor or a dentist.
Say where it hurts and describe symptoms with I’ve got, My… hurts, I feel.
Understand the doctor’s questions and advice (How long…?, You should…).
Manage at the pharmacy (prescription, how often to take medicine).

texte: On the phone: “I’d like to make an appointment with Dr Patel, please.” (for a doctor, always “an appointment”, never “a rendez-vous”). They may ask: “Is it urgent?” / “Can you come in at ten tomorrow?”

Places: in the UK you see “the doctor” or “the GP” (general practitioner, a family doctor) at the “surgery” or “health centre”; in the US you go to “the doctor’s office”. In an emergency: “A&E” (UK) / “the ER” (US) = the hospital emergency department.
We say “go to the doctor’s”, “go to the dentist’s”: the ’s means “the doctor’s place / surgery”.
exemples: I’d like to make an appointment with the doctor, please. — Is tomorrow morning OK?
Booking by phone.
I need to see a dentist. I’ve got terrible toothache.
toothache = pain in a tooth.
If it’s an emergency, call 999 in the UK or 911 in the US.
Emergency numbers.

texte: Three main structures. 1) “I’ve got a + -ache word”: “I’ve got a headache”, “a stomach ache”, “a backache”, “earache”, “toothache” (in the UK, earache and toothache often have no “a”).
2) “My + body part + hurts”: “My back hurts.” “My feet hurt.” (plural → hurt). You can also say “My leg is sore.” / “I’ve got a sore throat.”
3) “It hurts when…”: “It hurts when I walk.” Careful: English uses a possessive (“my arm”), not “the”: “My arm hurts”, not “The arm hurts me”.

lignes: I’ve got a sore + body part

exemples: I’ve got a headache and a sore throat.
Two problems with I’ve got.
My back hurts when I sit for a long time.
My + body part + hurts.
Where does it hurt? — Here, in my chest.
The doctor’s question.

texte: With “I’ve got”: “I’ve got a cold”, “a cough”, “a temperature / a fever” (“a temperature” is common in the UK), “the flu”, “a rash” (red spots on the skin).
With “I feel” + adjective: “I feel sick” (UK: you want to vomit; US: “sick” = ill in general), “I feel dizzy” (the room seems to turn), “I feel tired”, “I don’t feel well”.
For how long, use the present perfect (lesson 51) with “for” or “since”: “I’ve had a cough for three days.” / “I’ve felt sick since yesterday.” Don’t say “I have a cough since three days”.
exemples: I don’t feel well. I think I’ve got the flu.
the flu = influenza.
I’ve had a temperature since Monday.
since + starting point.
I feel dizzy when I stand up.
I feel + adjective.

texte: Common questions: “What’s the matter?” / “What seems to be the problem?”, “How long have you had it?”, “Are you taking any medicine?”, “Are you allergic to anything?”
The examination: “Can you open your mouth?”, “I’m going to take your temperature / your blood pressure.”

Advice with “should” / “shouldn’t” (lesson 56): “You should stay in bed for two days.” “You shouldn’t go to work.” “Drink plenty of water.” And the medicine: “I’ll give you a prescription.” (a paper from the doctor to get medicine).
exemples: What seems to be the problem? — I’ve had a bad cough for a week.
A polite opening question.
You should rest and drink plenty of water.
plenty of = a lot of.
You shouldn’t do any sport for a few days.
Negative advice.

texte: The shop: “the chemist’s” or “the pharmacy” (UK), “the drugstore” or “the pharmacy” (US). The person: “the pharmacist” (or “the chemist” in the UK).
Useful phrases: “Have you got anything for a cough?”, “I’ve got a prescription from my doctor.”, “How often should I take it?”
Instructions: “Take two tablets three times a day, after meals.” “medicine” is often uncountable: “some medicine”; “drugs” can also mean illegal drugs, so “medicine” is safer.
exemples: Have you got anything for a sore throat?
anything for + problem.
Take one tablet twice a day for five days.
twice = two times.
Can I take this medicine with food?
A safety question.
sections.note: To wish someone a quick recovery: “Get well soon!” or “I hope you feel better soon.”

formule: I’ve got a headache / a sore throat / a cold. · My back hurts. · I feel sick / dizzy. · I’ve had it for three days. · You should rest.
prononciation: “ache” /eɪk/ sounds like “make”: headache /ˈhedeɪk/, stomach ache /ˈstʌmək eɪk/.
“throat” /θrəʊt/: start with th (tongue between your teeth), then “rote”.
“medicine” /ˈmedsn/ or /ˈmedɪsn/: often two syllables in British English, “MED-sn”.
erreurs: I have mal at the head.
Pain in your head = a headache.
I have pain at the arm.
I have a cough since three days.
I’ve had a cough for three days.
I'd like a rendez-vous with the doctor.
I'd like an appointment with the doctor.
I’ve got a temperature. / I’ve got a fever.
Can you give me an ordonnance?
Could you give me a prescription?

dialogue.contexte: Kofi, a Ghanaian student in Bristol, goes to see a GP because he doesn’t feel well.
lignes: Good morning. What seems to be the problem?
I don’t feel well. I’ve got a sore throat and a headache.
How long have you had these symptoms?
For three days. And I’ve had a temperature since last night.
OK. Can you open your mouth? … It’s a throat infection. I’ll give you a prescription.
How often should I take the tablets?
Three times a day, after meals. And you should stay at home for two days.
“doctor” can be used to address the doctor.

mots: I’ve got an appointment at half past nine.
a fixed time to see a doctor or someone at work
He’s had a cough for a week.
the noise you make to push air out of your throat
a body heat that is higher than normal (UK)
I feel dizzy when I stand up.
You need a prescription for this medicine.
a doctor’s paper that lets you get medicine
a small, hard piece of medicine
You should rest for a few days.
to relax and sleep to get better

exercices.consigne: Complete with “I’ve got a”, “My … hurts” or “I feel”.

items: I’d like to make an ___ with Dr Brown.
I’ve had a headache ___ two days.
Take one tablet three times a ___.
Have you got anything ___ a cold?

exercices.consigne: Who says this: the doctor or the patient?
items: What seems to be the problem?
How long have you had it?
How often should I take it?

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: I’ve got an ache of stomach.
I have a temperature since yesterday.
I’ve had a temperature since yesterday.
I’d like to make a rendez-vous.
I’d like to make an appointment.
You should to drink plenty of water.
You should drink plenty of water.

exercices.consigne: You phone the doctor’s surgery, then describe your symptoms to the doctor (5 to 6 sentences): where it hurts, since when, how you feel.
items: Hello, I’d like to make an appointment with the doctor, please. It’s quite urgent. … Good morning, doctor. I don’t feel well. I’ve got a bad cough and a sore throat, and my chest hurts when I cough. I’ve had these symptoms for four days. I’ve also had a temperature since yesterday and I feel very tired. I’m not allergic to anything.

a_retenir: an appointment; at the doctor’s; emergency = A&E (UK) / the ER (US).
Pain: I’ve got a headache / stomach ache / sore throat · My back hurts · It hurts when I…
Symptoms: I’ve got a cold / a cough / a temperature · I feel sick / dizzy · I don’t feel well.
How long: I’ve had a cough for three days / since Monday (present perfect).
Advice: You should rest. You shouldn’t go to work. Pharmacy: Take two tablets three times a day.
